passage:
Subject: my timetable is ruined
Siddharth bhaiya,
You know my board-exam timetable, the one with green for physics, blue for maths and every half hour planned till March. On Saturday Mausi's flight was delayed, and we all went to fetch her from the airport at midnight. I lost the whole Sunday to sleep. I felt so guilty that I cancelled my cricket for the next two weeks to "pay it back" and stayed up till two redoing the colour codes. Today I could barely read one page. Amma says I'm punishing myself. Maybe. You topped your boards. Did you ever lose a day? How did you not panic?
Saurabh

qa.q: What colour did Saurabh use for physics?
qa.a: Green for physics.

qa.q: Why did Saurabh cancel cricket for two weeks?
qa.a: Saurabh felt guilty about the lost Sunday and wanted to "pay it back", treating rest as something to be punished.

qa.q: What went wrong after the lost Sunday, and what could Saurabh try instead?
qa.a: Staying up till two to redo the codes left Saurabh barely able to read; simply moving the lost work into the coming week would cost less.

qa.q: How might Amma feel watching Saurabh this week?
qa.a: Amma seems worried to see hard work turning into self-punishment, which is why she says so out loud.

grounding: A teenager with a colour-coded exam timetable feels guilty over one unplanned day and turns the plan into self-punishment.

passage:
Afreen asked, "Dhruv, why did you look like a ghost all last week?"
Honestly, Afreen, the planner is the best thing about me. Six colours, every chapter mapped, and I've never missed a deadline. But last Tuesday Nani turned eighty and the house filled with cousins. No studying. I smiled through the cake and felt sick the whole time, like I was stealing hours. That night I set an alarm for four to make up for it, and the next night too. By Thursday I was reading the same paragraph again and again and snapping at my little brother. You know what finally hit me? The planner had no row for Nani. I'd made a plan that could only break, never bend. So now I'm trying something scary: Sundays left blank.

qa.q: How many colours does Dhruv's planner use?
qa.a: Six colours, every chapter mapped.

qa.q: What was Dhruv feeling during Nani's birthday cake?
qa.a: Dhruv felt guilty and sick, as if the family hours were being stolen from study.

qa.q: What turning point does Dhruv reach about the planner?
qa.a: Dhruv notices it had no row for Nani and decides to leave Sundays blank, so the plan can bend instead of break.

qa.q: How might Dhruv's little brother have experienced that week?
qa.a: Being snapped at by a tired older sibling probably hurt, with no way of knowing it came from the four o'clock alarms.

grounding: A teenager proud of a detailed study planner feels guilty after an unplanned family day and answers it with punishing early alarms before seeing the plan must bend.

passage:
Saturday, 11.40 p.m.
The timetable said: Chemistry 4 to 7, Maths 8 to 10. Instead: Lokesh's cousin's wedding. Mummy said I had to come, so I sat at the reception with my green highlighter in my pocket like an idiot. Lokesh kept saying, 'Relax, it's one evening.' But I could feel the chemistry slots going red in my head. Came home and crossed out today's box so hard the pen went through. Then I wrote: Sunday, 6 a.m. to 11 p.m., no breaks, no cricket for a week. Now I'm looking at it and it looks like a punishment, not a plan. Is that what it's turned into? The colour-coding used to make me feel calm. Tonight it just makes me feel guilty.
Francis

qa.q: What did Francis's timetable plan for Saturday?
qa.a: Chemistry 4 to 7 and Maths 8 to 10.

qa.q: How did Francis feel after missing the planned study?
qa.a: Francis felt guilty and tense, crossing out the day so hard the pen went through.

qa.q: What could Francis do instead of the no-breaks Sunday?
qa.a: Spread the missed chemistry over a couple of spare slots in the week and keep cricket, treating the wedding as a normal interruption rather than a failure.

qa.q: How might Lokesh have seen Francis at the wedding?
qa.a: Lokesh probably saw a friend too tense to enjoy one evening, and kept trying to help Francis relax.

grounding: Shows a teenager whose disciplined, colour-coded timetable turns into guilt and self-punishment when a family event interrupts it.

Harsha: u ok? u left the group call
Sumit: nani got admitted this morning, was at the hospital all day
Harsha: oh no. is she ok??
Sumit: stable. doctors say she'll be fine
Sumit: but i lost the whole day. physics numericals ch 4-6 were today's slot
Sumit: my timetable is colour coded till march and today is just a red hole
Harsha: sumit. ur nani was in hospital
Sumit: i know. i still feel sick about it
Sumit: planning to do today + tomorrow's tonight
Harsha: it's 11. u'll be a zombie for the mock
Sumit: then i'll have failed at 2 things
Harsha: or u sleep, and we split ch 4-6 on sunday. i'll bring my notes
Sumit: ...ok. maybe
Harsha: not maybe. sleep

qa.q: Why did Sumit miss the day's study slot?
qa.a: Nani got admitted to hospital and Sumit was there all day.

qa.q: What was Sumit feeling about the 'red hole' in the timetable?
qa.a: Sumit felt guilty and anxious, even sick, about losing one day despite the reason.

qa.q: What did Harsha suggest, and why is it wiser than studying all night?
qa.a: Sleep tonight and split the chapters on Sunday with shared notes; it protects the mock and stops the plan turning into a punishment.

qa.q: How might Harsha feel reading that Sumit plans to study late into the night?
qa.a: Harsha seems worried, pushing firmly for sleep because a worn-out Sumit would struggle in the mock.

grounding: Shows a teenager with a strict colour-coded timetable who feels guilty and plans to punish themselves after a family emergency interrupts it.

passage: On the wall above Kishore's cot in Motihari hung a timetable in four colours: blue for maths, green for biology, red for revision, yellow for rest. There was not much yellow. On Saturday his father's back gave out and someone had to mind the grain shop. Kishore sat behind the scales all day, weighing rice, his biology notes open under the counter. He read the same page nine times. That night he lit the lamp and began squeezing the whole lost day into the night, determined to pay back every hour. Pankaj, passing, saw the light at one in the morning and tapped on the window. 'Still?' 'I wasted today.' 'You ran the shop so your father could rest. That's wasted?' Kishore looked at the colours. For the first time the chart looked less like a plan than a bill he owed.

qa.q: Which colour on Kishore's timetable stood for rest?
qa.a: Yellow.

qa.q: What was Kishore feeling when he began paying back the lost hours at night?
qa.a: He felt guilty and driven, as if helping at the shop were a debt he had to punish himself for.

qa.q: What could Kishore change in his timetable after this?
qa.a: Add more yellow and a few spare slots for days like this, so an interruption means moving work, not staying up half the night.

qa.q: How does Pankaj see Kishore's Saturday?
qa.a: Pankaj sees a day well spent helping his father, not wasted, and is worried to find him still up at one.

grounding: Shows a teenager whose disciplined timetable becomes self-punishment when a family need interrupts it.

passage: In Istanbul, Camila, sixteen, had her exam timetable taped above her desk: blue for chemistry, green for history, every hour colour-coded. Then an earthquake drill and a power cut wiped out two whole days of study. On the second night she sat up till two, copying notes by phone torchlight, furious with herself. "I'm so behind. I don't deserve a break." Her friend Zeynep came over with simit and found her red-eyed. "You're the most disciplined person I know. But you're punishing yourself for a power cut." Camila laughed shakily. Zeynep helped her redraw the week with two catch-up slots and one free evening. That night, Camila slept eight hours, and felt guilty only for about ten minutes.

qa.q: What wiped out two days of Camila's study?
qa.a: An earthquake drill and a power cut.

qa.q: How did Camila feel about losing two days?
qa.a: She felt guilty and furious with herself, as if she didn't deserve a break.

qa.q: What did Zeynep help Camila do?
qa.a: Zeynep helped her redraw the timetable with catch-up slots and a free evening, instead of punishing herself.

qa.q: How does Zeynep see Camila's discipline?
qa.a: Zeynep sees it as a real strength, but worries it has turned into self-punishment.

grounding: Shows a disciplined teenager who colour-codes her study and feels guilty when life interrupts, and a friend helping her see rigid plans have become self-punishment.
